fa: An unauthorized adaptation of Dracula so blatant that a lawsuit from Bram Stoker's estate ordered all copies destroyed; surviving prints preserved what became one of cinema's most influential horror films.
Its jagged, painted-on sets pioneered German Expressionist cinema and influenced the visual language of horror and film noir for decades.
Bela Lugosi's performance defined the modern image of the vampire and launched Universal Pictures' entire classic monster movie era.
Boris Karloff's monster makeup became so iconic that it is still instantly recognizable a century later, despite Karloff receiving no line of dialogue for much of the film.
Hitchcock bought up copies of the source novel to preserve the twist, and famously required cinemas to bar latecomers from entering once the film had started.
Achieved its unsettling attack scenes almost entirely with trained birds and mechanical effects, decades before CGI existed.
Its slow-building paranoia about a sinister apartment building made it a template for psychological horror that trusts dread over jump scares.

n_es: La noche de los muertos vivientes
fa: Made on a shoestring budget, it single-handedly created the modern zombie genre and its rules that countless later films would follow.
Reports of fainting audience members at its 1973 release turned it into a cultural phenomenon; it remains one of the few horror films nominated for the Best Picture Oscar.
Its folk-horror atmosphere of pagan ritual on a remote Scottish island inspired an entire subgenre that resurfaced decades later.
Despite its brutal reputation, it contains almost no on-screen gore; its terror comes largely from suggestion, sound design and relentless pacing.
Its saturated primary-color lighting and pulsing prog-rock score by Goblin turned a ballet academy into one of horror's most visually striking nightmares.
David Lynch's surreal debut, shot over several years on a minuscule budget, became a defining work of body-horror and midnight-movie cinema.
A haunted-house film unlike any other, mixing cartoonish special effects and dreamlike logic that made it a cult favorite decades after its release.
Made for around 300,000 dollars, it became one of the most profitable independent films ever and established many conventions of the slasher genre.
H.R. Giger's biomechanical creature design gave science-fiction horror an entirely new visual vocabulary that is still imitated today.
Based on a supposedly true haunting, its enormous commercial success sparked a decades-long franchise and debate over how much of its story was fabricated.
Kubrick reportedly demanded over 100 takes of some scenes; its unsettling use of the Steadicam through the Overlook Hotel's corridors became legendary.

n_es: Un hombre lobo americano en Londres
fa: Its transformation sequence, achieved entirely with practical makeup effects, won the very first Academy Award given for makeup.
Its suburban setting made supernatural horror feel close to home, and its production was later shadowed by tabloid stories about an alleged curse.
Its shape-shifting alien creature effects, built almost entirely with practical animatronics, are still studied by effects artists as a benchmark decades later.
Its premise, that a killer could reach victims through their dreams, made sleep itself feel dangerous and launched one of horror's most recognizable villains.
Blended slapstick comedy with gruesome horror so effectively that it helped define the horror-comedy genre for the decades that followed.
Adapted by author Clive Barker from his own novella, its intricate puzzle box and Cenobite creatures introduced a distinctly gothic, S&M-tinged strain of horror.
Turned a children's toy into a horror icon, sparking a long-running franchise and renewed public unease about dolls in general.
Kathy Bates won an Academy Award for playing a fan who holds an injured novelist captive, proving horror could earn top acting honors.
One of only three films in history to sweep all five major Academy Awards, remarkable for a film built around a serial killer thriller.
Set against Chicago's Cabrini-Green housing project, it used urban legend and social commentary to give slasher horror unusual depth.
Its cursed videotape premise ignited the J-horror boom and inspired a wave of American remakes throughout the 2000s.
Its slow-burn first half plays almost like a romantic drama before an infamous tonal shift that shocked festival audiences worldwide.

n_es: El proyecto de la bruja de Blair
fa: Made for roughly 60,000 dollars and marketed as if it were real found footage, it kickstarted the modern found-footage horror genre.
Its fog-bound gothic mansion and slow-building dread earned it comparisons to classic ghost stories rather than modern jump-scare horror.
Set during the Spanish Civil War, del Toro blended ghost story and wartime tragedy in a film he has called a spiritual sibling to Pan's Labyrinth.
Its fast-moving, rage-infected creatures reinvented the zombie genre, replacing the traditional shambling undead with sprinting horror.
Shot in just 18 days on a tiny budget, its moral traps premise spawned one of the most commercially successful horror franchises ever made.
Blended dark fairy tale fantasy with the horrors of fascist Spain, and remains one of the rare horror-adjacent films to win multiple Academy Awards.
Its found-footage format, following a news crew locked inside a quarantined apartment building, made it one of Spain's most successful horror exports.
Made for around 15,000 dollars and shot largely in the director's own house, it became one of the most profitable films ever made relative to its budget.
A wintry, melancholy vampire story about lonely children that critics frequently rank among the greatest vampire films ever made.
Sam Raimi's return to horror after a decade of blockbusters brought back the gleeful, over-the-top style of his earlier Evil Dead films.
Relied on atmosphere and sound design over graphic violence, helping usher in a new wave of PG-13-friendly studio horror.
Written by Joss Whedon and Drew Goddard as an affectionate deconstruction of horror movie tropes, twisting the genre's own rules against itself.
Based on paranormal investigators Ed and Lorraine Warren, it launched one of the most successful horror franchises of the 21st century.
Its premise of a slow, unstoppable supernatural pursuer became widely read as an allegory, while its synth score revived a distinctly retro horror sound.
A grieving single mother's battle with a storybook monster was embraced by critics as a rare horror film built on genuine emotional depth.
Its story of twin boys suspicious of their bandaged mother was Austria's official submission for the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film.

n: A Girl Walks Home Alone at Night
fa: Billed as 'the first Iranian vampire western', shot in black and white with Persian dialogue despite being filmed in California.
Its dialogue was constructed largely from 17th-century historical texts to recreate authentic Puritan New England speech.
Jordan Peele's directorial debut used horror to explore race in America and won him the Academy Award for Best Original Screenplay.
Weaves fairy-tale imagery through the real horrors faced by children orphaned by Mexico's drug war, earning praise from Guillermo del Toro himself.
Toni Collette's performance as a grieving mother unraveling was widely called one of the greatest in horror history, despite being overlooked at major awards.
Built almost entirely around silence, with sound itself becoming the source of danger for its sound-hunting alien creatures.
A hospice nurse's religious devotion curdles into obsession in this British debut that critics compared to Taxi Driver for its unreliable narration.
Almost entirely set in broad Scandinavian daylight, it proved horror does not require darkness to unsettle an audience.
Shot in black and white on a nearly square aspect ratio, its two-hander of dueling lighthouse keepers became an instant arthouse horror classic.
Follows Sudanese refugees haunted by a supernatural presence in their new English home, blending trauma narrative with haunted-house horror.
Made by two former YouTubers on a modest budget, it became one of A24's highest-grossing horror releases through purely word-of-mouth buzz.
Curry Barker's feature directorial debut follows a shy music store worker who buys a cursed toy to win a friend's love, only for her devotion to spiral into something far darker.
Directed by Kane Parsons at just 20 years old in his feature debut, it expanded his own viral YouTube web series adapting the 'Backrooms' creepypasta into a full studio release from A24.
